newsitem.title: USA: New UPI chief outlines plans for profit.
newsitem.headline: New UPI chief outlines plans for profit.

text.p: United Press International named a new chief executive Wednesday who said he plans to make the troubled international wire service a profitable organisation after years of losses.

James Adams, who came to UPI in 1992 as Washington bureau chief, was previously managing editor of the Sunday Times of London, which he turned into a money-maker for owner Rupert Murdoch by installing new technology and boosting productivity.

Adams said he hopes to bring the same ethos to UPI. Though the wire service has a long, proud journalistic history, it has also been unprofitable for years, changed ownership frequently, and in May even saw its former chief executive, Earl Brian, sentenced to prison for bank and securities fraud.
"A series of independent operators were running UPI without concerns for the bottom line," said Adams. "The bottom line has now been made of singular importance."

The current owners will not support UPI's losses indefinitely. "The Saudi investors who bought us in 1993 have put in tens of millions of dollars to sustain losses that had gone on," said Adams. "But there's no reason they will continue to do so. They want to make a profit."
In his new post, which takes effect on June 16, he will succeed acting CEO Paul Heigl.
UPI will be market-driven, Adams said. "My sense is that the role of the traditional worldwide news organisation is coming to an end. You can't sit back and dictate what the world sees and reads."
UPI, he said, will be focused on three areas -- print, the Internet, and radio -- where Adams feels the chances for success are greatest.
UPI reports are already in many places on the World Wide Web, and Adams said he was also planning to expand the company's outlets for radio news in the United States.
As for print, he said, "Now that we've cut staff, we don't say print is finished. We say go for print and be very specific about what you do."
That means joint-ventures according to Adams, two of which should be announced shortly, one before the end of the month. But Adams declined to provide specifics.

Profitability in newspaper services also mean rearranging news resources to reflect what the market wants, said Adams. For instance he's planning an investigative news unit, and reducing what he called "very expensive " coverage emanating from South Asia.
But Adams said he doesn't plan on further cuts among UPI's editorial staff of 260 full-time employees and "hundreds" of stringers.
"There have already been a series of cuts, without the creativity to move forward," he said. "My remit is to grow the organisation."
